I've been out of the loop - could someone ELI5 what's going on with it? I'd Google it, but don't want to spend hours wading through political soundbites to find "just the facts ma'am".
What's going on with the Iran nuclear deal?
Israel is mad. Obama is busy high giving the countless other nations including many EU allies who have been wary of Israel's brand of pushy bullying for a while.

The current status is as such: Iran and the US (along with 6 other countries) have agreed to a deal, pending approval by all of the various parliamentary and congressional folks for each country (for example, the US congress has 60 days to vote on approval of the agreement. Other countries have similar periods for discussion) Everything is in limbo until that process ends. The "fact" part of the deal has already been hammered out by the negotiators, and now it's just the almost entirely political process of internal debates about Iran's trustworthiness and nit-picking on things that opponents don't agree with.

As for the deal itself:

The deal is around 100 pages, much of it technical appendices, but the overall plan is to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons in the short/medium term. This is done a few ways:

Step 1: reduce uranium enrichment capabilities

enrichment means separating Uranium-235 out from other, non-useful uranium isotopes. Bombs need the U235 levels in the material to be around 90% total volume. Most countries enrich to around 5% for power plants. Iran currently has enriched material at around the 20% mark.

Iran has agreed to cut it's number of operating centrifuges in half, dramatically slowing the rate at which they can enrich uranium by that process. They have also agreed to limit enrichment to 3.7% for new material, and to cap how much material they can stockpile to around 600lbs (a reduction of around 98%).

Step 2: the Plutonium processes

Uranium isn't the only material you can use for bombs, there's also plutonium. Iran was building a reactor in Arak that would take Uranium fuel, and as a byproduct turn it into Plutonium-239. The Deal requires Iran to mothball the original reactor core (which would produce weapons grade material), require them to change the design of the functional Arak reactor core so that it will not produce weapons grade materials, waste materials from it (which could be processed into weapons grade material) are required to be shipped out of the country. Iran is barred from building any new heavy water reactors for 15 years.

Step 3: No cheating!

Iran has agreed to provide the International Atomic Energy Agency access and information regarding its nuclear program, and to allow the agency to investigate suspicious sites anywhere in the country. Inspectors will also have access to the supply chain (including uranium mines and mills, centrifuge manufacturing and storage facilities) The limits on enrichment, research and development last for 15 years. Some inspections and transparency measures will remain in place for 25 years.

I think the main arguments against the deal that I've seen are that:

1) it doesn't permanently end anything. Most of the restrictions are 15 years and that's it.

2) the "breakout" time if Iran decided "screw it, we want a bomb" with the deal in place is only about a year. This is because Iran isn't required to destroy or disassemble any of it's equipment or reactors, just shut them down and promise not to use them.

3) somewhere, at some point, someone got it in their heads that the deal would include 24x7x365 snap inspections of anything in Iran. From what I understand, this was never reality, and inspections would always have a lead time of a few days to a week. People expecting the former are rather upset that they have to accept the latter.

4) once all the deal stipulations are adhered to and sanctions are lifted (between 2-8 years, I've seen) Iran will be have access to funding, resources and technology that it currently can't access, leaving them in a much better place to build a bomb should they decide to renege on the deal. People seem to want less carrot and a bigger stick.

5) The deal only changes Iran's Nuclear programs, not it's political, social or ideological structures. Israel, among others, has problems with this.

Iran has a nuclear program, and tries to be stubborn about what it is allowed to do. Some countries are wary that it could mean they could have access to nuclear weapons (the same way Canada is close to develop it). A bunch of sanction were placed on Iran because it defied the West into saying that they were allowed to have a peaceful nuclear program as per the treaty, without having to bow at the extra demand of the West. Now those sanctions are lifted in exchange for a large portion of the stockpile of uranium.
